evidence: The staff sounds C, D, F-sharp and A at this onset, which is a plain dominant seventh chord on D in third inversion, with C in the bass. The label Ger7/bV names a German sixth chord, a type of augmented-sixth chord, applied to the flattened fifth degree, and its expansion re-spells those same four pitch classes as E-double-flat, G-flat, B-double-flat and C. The re-spelling is enharmonic, meaning it preserves every sounding pitch while changing how each note is written, and the arithmetic itself is faithful to the annotation standard, because the corpus parses the label into the numeral vii with the diminished form, the figured-bass figure 7, the alteration b3 and the relative root V/bV, which is the equivalence the standard defines for German sixth chords. The question is therefore not whether the expansion was computed correctly but whether the annotator was entitled to override the composer's notated spelling: the annotation standard this corpus follows, the Digital and Cognitive Musicology Lab harmonic annotation guidelines, contains no rule about when a notated spelling may be overridden in the sections that govern Roman numerals, relative keys and augmented-sixth chords, so the re-spelling is an unguided annotator judgement rather than a defect. That re-spelling is what pushes the chord outside the naming systems that consume this data.
